In the middle of Taylor Swift's Eras Tour, her then-boyfriend, Travis Kelce, materialized onstage wearing a top hat and grinning ear-to-ear. He clicked his heels, cradled Swift in his arms, and mimed putting makeup on her face during a well-rehearsed skit, hitting all his marks as a member of her supporting cast.
While tens of thousands of fans in London's Wembley Stadium screamed their approval, none had shelled out money for tickets to see Kelce. His cameo was the mere cherry on top of Swift's monumental career achievement: She'd set an attendance record for the venue and generated an estimated $1 billion for the UK economy.
Not that Kelce seemed to mind playing second fiddle. In fact, he said it was "an honor" to dip his toe into Swift's world, casting himself as a superfan who got luckier than most.
"You can do no wrong when Taylor's onstage," Kelce said on his podcast. "She's the best to do it."
Kelce is a star in his own right, an athlete on track for the NFL Hall of Fame. Yet Kelce's reported net worth is dwarfed by Swift's multibillion-dollar fortune, and this summer's headlines about his return to football can't resist shoehorning in a mention of his and Swift's recent wedding.
Off the field, Kelce's prestige is not threatened by Swift's success but is perhaps even bolstered by it. He belongs to a new wave of secure Hollywood husbands: male celebrities whose enthusiastic endorsement of their high-earning wives makes them more endearing and, crucially, more bankable.
Think: Tom Holland, Spider-Man himself, interrupting his own interview at a "Spider-Man" premiere to admire the glamorous arrival of his wife, Zendaya. (This has happened not just once, but many times.) Holland also told Men's Health that he doesn't join Zendaya on non-Marvel-related red carpets because "it's not my moment, it's her moment."
Or consider the musician Benny Blanco, who said he's so afraid of flying that he literally took a boat across the Atlantic Ocean to lay eyes on his billionaire wife, Selena Gomez, who's currently in London filming her Emmy-winning TV show. "The things we do for love," he wrote on TikTok.
This pattern offers a refreshing contrast to the more common reality, which is that divorce rates in heterosexual couples rise significantly when a woman is more professionally successful than her male partner.
It may also offer an escapist balm for the women in question. Celebrity culture thrives by reflecting our own desires like a gilded mirror — and husbands like Kelce, Holland, and Blanco represent an alluring ideal for women at a time when many are outpacing their male counterparts in the labor market. Women outnumber men in medical school and law school; they earn more bachelor's degrees; and they hold more jobs in the US as of March, according to a survey conducted by the Indeed Hiring Lab.
"That concept of a supportive husband is really appealing to women in 2026," Mike Fahey, the founder and CEO of the PR agency Fahey Communications, told Business Insider. Plus, famous hype husbands who are loving and supportive enjoy the added bonus of being "more marketable," Fahey said.
A female breadwinner isn't exactly a new phenomenon, but as women accumulate more cultural and economic clout — and as prominent men publicly celebrate that trend — the strict "alpha male" archetype loses its luster.
"We're reimagining what masculinity looks like," Fahey said. "As more of those couples take A-plus-list status, others follow suit. You just need one trailblazer to really change the game for the rest of Hollywood."
'They're more than just the alpha male. They're the modern male.'
The social media era has transformed celebrity branding, turning descriptors like "real" and "relatable" into high praise. Now more than ever, it pays for celebrities to put their dimensions on display, be it via Instagram posts, red carpet appearances, or paparazzi shots. One of the best ways to do so is by giving fans a glimpse into their relationships.
"This is a really important place for men to show that they're more than just the roles they play," Fahey said. "They're more than just the alpha male. They're the modern male."
Take someone like the rapper A$AP Rocky, who rose to fame with songs like "Peso" and "F**kin' Problems," which feature lyrics in which he brags about his groupies and his own pretty face. Rocky still releases popular, braggadocious music — and his latest album, "Don't Be Dumb," debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in January — but now, he also spends a lot of time gushing about Rihanna, his longtime partner and the mother of his children, not to mention a beloved hitmaker and Fenty Beauty billionaire.
"So much better when you got 'the one,'" Rocky told GQ when he confirmed their relationship. "She amounts to probably, like, a million of the other ones."
Unlike the trite "wife guy" archetype — the kind of man who builds and sustains his entire image on his marriage, to the point that it can read as performative — Hollywood's hype husbands have plenty going for them on their own. Kelce has Super Bowl rings, and Holland has record-breaking box-office achievements. Blanco made hit songs like Rihanna's "Diamonds" and Katy Perry's "California Gurls" long before he teamed up with his pop-star wife for a collaborative album, 2025's "I Said I Love You First."
Peter Mancusi, a PR professional and communications professor at Northeastern University, said the distinction comes down to self-sufficiency and confidence: It's not "I need you," but "I want you."
"It's not like these men are drafting their wives to become famous themselves. They're already, in their own realms, famous," Mancusi explained.
"Confidence is really about doing what these men are doing, which is supporting their partners," he continued. "It's to say, 'I'm confident enough in who I am to be very supportive of her spectacular career.'"
Want to win over female audiences? Supporting your wife is a good place to start.
In Rob Sheffield's book, "Heartbreak Is the National Anthem: How Taylor Swift Reinvented Pop Music," about Swift's impact on the music industry, he quotes Smokey Robinson: "Women make show business," the singer-songwriter and producer told Rolling Stone in 1979. "Men contribute to the thing, but women actually make show business happen."
Sheffield argues that Swift knows this all too well, but I would argue that her husband Kelce does, too. When he proudly declares that his favorite Taylor Swift song is "Blank Space," or he's caught filming the Eras Tour on his phone, Swifties are eager to rally behind him. He becomes one of them.
"Being this famous football player and having this supportive, softer side to him — he's into the music, into what his wife is about — is very appealing, especially to women," Mancusi said. "He's got unlimited possibilities because of his relationship."
"Getting women on your side makes your brand much stronger."Mike Fahey, founder and CEO of Fahey Communications
Women and girls are the driving force behind fan culture — often as early champions of male celebrities they find charming and non-threatening, from The Beatles to Harry Styles to the stars of "Heated Rivalry." History shows that winning over female audiences can be a fast track to stardom.
"I think that women are more likely to click 'Follow,' they're more likely to click 'Like,' they're more likely to visit your TikTok shop," Fahey said. "Getting women on your side makes your brand much stronger. It makes your longevity much stronger. It makes your marketability much stronger and your prospects limitless."
Melvin L. Williams, a communications and media studies professor at Pace University, agreed that famous men like Kelce, Blanco, and Callum Turner, who recently wed pop juggernaut Dua Lipa, are "keenly aware of the economic benefits" of wooing the crowds who flock to their famous wives.
"Each man's next business venture or media appearance has the possibility of a highly profitable endorsement from a notable figure like Selena Gomez, Dua Lipa, or Taylor Swift," Williams said.
Indeed, after Kelce began dating Swift, NFL viewership spiked — particularly among teenage girls — and sales of Kelce's jersey surged nearly 400% when Swift made her first game-day appearance. Kelce's brother, former NFL player Jason Kelce, has credited Swift with introducing their family to a whole new demographic.
Meanwhile, Blanco's joint album with Gomez sold more in its first week than any other album in his discography, and rumors are swirling that Turner — who was previously best known for starring in the embattled "Harry Potter" spinoff series, "Fantastic Beasts" — is being eyed as the next James Bond.
So whatever you want to call it — modern masculinity, savvy branding, or simply being a good husband — being in love with a commercial juggernaut has its perks. For Hollywood's hype husbands, a happy wife makes for a lucrative life.

A Canadian airline cancelled a flight from Victoria to Toronto after a child refused to wear a seatbelt.
The child was standing in their chair as the 6 August Porter Airlines flight taxied towards the runway, the airline said. Repeated attempts by an accompanying parent and crew to secure the child in their seat failed, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark as “the aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition”, it added.
Brad Cicero, a spokesperson for the airline, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) that all passengers had to disembark, as the time needed to remove only the child and their parent and refile paperwork meant the plane could not take off before the airport closed at 12:30am.
“We apologise for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day,” he told the broadcaster.
Passenger Aryeh Kozuch told the Canadian Press that the child was not being unruly, and that online comments admonishing the parents did not “empathetically capture the situation”.
“They just kept hiding under their seat,” he said. “If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath.”
“This was a child that was in a tube with 150 people … They’re obviously terrified, and their response was to try and hide under the seat in front of them,” he said. “That’s so different than a kid running around and screaming.”
Hillary Hertzberg, another passenger, said the airline could have acted faster. “It took for ever,” Hertzberg told CBC. “The kid eventually got off the plane at 11.30 so we had been on the flight for almost an hour at that point.”
Porter Airlines said passengers were rebooked on a different flight the following day.

Quick Answer
Round Sync is a free, open-source Android app that brings Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, and dozens of other cloud services into one place. It lets you browse, move, sync, stream, and encrypt files without ads, paid tiers, or separate apps.
These days, no amount of storage is sufficient, as everything, right from images and videos to apps, has become quite hefty in size. I have lost count of the different cloud storage apps I have installed on my phone right now. I use Google Drive for work, OneDrive for my personal media, Dropbox for something I used years ago, etc. Every single one of them wants its own app, its own login screen, its own little corner on my phone’s home screen. The worst part is that none of them talk to each other.
That is exactly what Round Sync does, and it fills the gap. This free Android app lets you connect pretty much every cloud storage app and manage all of them from a single app. Let us know more about it.
What is Round Sync?
Round Sync is a free, open-source Android app that lets you manage all of your cloud storage in one place. It is a unified file browser that requires no premium tier, shows you no ads, and no “upgrade to unlock more” nonsense. It is built on top of Rclone, which is a widely respected open-source command-line tool that has been the backbone of cloud management on Linux and other platforms for years. What Round Sync does is take that Rclone command-line tool and wrap it in an actual Android interface that a regular person can tap through without ever touching a terminal.
Enough of the technical aspect of the app (which a normal user wouldn’t even care for); let us talk about the main reason you would want to keep this app installed on your phone. Since it is built on Rclone, it inherits support for dozens of cloud storage backends, be it Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Box, pCloud, Mega, Amazon S3, Backblaze B2, and self-hosted options like Nextcloud and WebDAV servers, among many others.
While most of them require an easy guided setup screen inside the app, for others, you need to import the Rclone configuration file. All in all, Round Sync eliminates the need to switch between multiple apps to check whether the file synced correctly. You open Round Sync once and see everything organized into folders side by side.
Round Sync treats cloud storage as local storage
For different cloud storage services, you need their separate apps on your phone. This not only eats up your phone’s storage but also makes it hard to make sure that everything is working perfectly fine. Moving files between two different cloud accounts means downloading them first locally and then re-uploading them manually. Round Sync ensures that you can list, view, download, upload, move, rename, and even delete files/folders directly. You can move things between remotes without that awkward double download-then-reupload dance.
It also plugs into the Android Storage Access Framework, so your cloud storage can show up inside other apps’ file pickers. Your gallery app, a document editor, whatever needs to browse or save a file. That is a small detail, but it is the kind of integration that separates an app that merely displays your cloud files from one that actually behaves like a part of the OS.
Here are some of the best features of Round Sync:
- Automated syncing: This is one feature that makes Round Sync genuinely useful. You can set up sync tasks that run automatically on a schedule. For instance, backing up your camera roll to Google Drive every night or mirror a work folder to OneDrive whenever you are on Wi-Fi. Once configured, you don’t have to think again.
- Stream, don’t just store: Round Sync isn’t just about copying and moving files around; you can also use it to stream media directly from your cloud storage. It can also serve your files and folders over FTP, HTTP, WebDAV, or DLNA. In simple terms, your phone can act as a media server, and you can point your phone to your smart TV or other device connected to the same network, and it will pull files straight from your phone.
- Privacy gets taken seriously here: If you are curious about how your files are handled by Round Sync, you should know that it supports 256-bit encryption through Rclone’s crypt remotes. This means that you can layer client-side encryption on top of any provider, including in the free tier on the provider’s servers.
- Works on almost all Android phones: Round Sync works on Android 7 or above, and ships builds for ARM, ARM64, x86, and x86_64 architectures. This means that it is not only available for flagship phones, but also for older phones as well. The UI follows the Material 3 design language, and there is proper dark theme support as well.
Getting Round Sync is super easy
Do note that, like most open-source Android apps, Round Sync isn’t available on the Google Play Store. But if you know, there are several Play Store alternatives like F-Droid, from where you can download this app. You can also download it from IzzyOnDroid, along with its GitHub release page.
Additionally, you need to sideload this app on your phone. If you don’t know a thing about sideloading apps on Android, this Samsung guide has everything you need to know about sideloading on Android. Setting up the app itself is quite straightforward. You get the app, install it, add a “remote” for each cloud storage you want to connect, and browse your files within a couple of minutes.
Should you use it?
If you’re the kind of person who only checks their cloud storage once a week, then Round Sync may not feel beneficial to you. The UI may not feel as polished as the one you get with Google Drive, and setting it up is a bit more manual compared to dedicated apps. However, if you manage multiple cloud storage accounts and want a one-stop shop for them, along with all the features you get on top, then Round Sync makes perfect sense. This also frees up your RAM since 5 different apps are not running in the background and eating up your RAM.

After doing three loops around the parking lot, you finally see a free spot. You step on the gas to claim it, but an SUV cuts in front of you and steals the space. You stomp on the brakes, jerking to a halt. You might forgive the other driver, but your Toyota remembers.
Later, as you drive home, your eyes wander to the restaurant that just opened on the corner. Your car loudly beeps you back to attention, the dashboard scolding, “keep eyes on the road.” Your car is watching you, and that hard stop and brief glance to the side are data sent directly to your car insurer, churning into an algorithm that decides your future premiums.
This surveillance model, called telematics, has become standard in auto insurance, as companies promise to save policyholders money if they agree to share their minute-to-minute driving data. They don’t actually save you money — a report by the Maryland Insurance Administration showed a mixed bag of premium changes with no real overall savings — but that hasn’t dissuaded companies.
As telematics grows in auto insurance, the human body is next. White House health officials and health insurance executives are pushing to bring a telematics model to mainstream medicine. “My vision is that every American is wearing a wearable in the next four years,” health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told House members in 2025. Kennedy claims devices that track your sleep, heart rate, glucose levels, and other metrics will help Americans “take control” of their health. And indeed, there are now countless wearables to track your vital bodily data — from your heart rate and daily steps to your ovulation and hormone levels.
But if the short history of telematics in the auto insurance taught us anything, it’s to be skeptical of any promises attached to shareable surveillance data, especially if corporations are involved.
Several key ethical questions for consumers remain unanswered.
First, there is not much evidence that wearables will lower any overall costs. If anything, wearables provide an ulterior profit motive for insurance companies.
Second, there are major privacy concerns embedded into the free sharing of minute-by-minute bodily data to corporations. How exactly will the data be used and how securely stored?
More broadly, the wearables endeavor promotes a highly individualized view of health that fails to acknowledge how social structures and inequalities shape our lifetime risk to disease. These risks could be attenuated with thoughtful health policy. Instead, the Department of Health and Human Services wants to slap an Apple Watch on your wrist.
Despite these unanswered questions, health and life insurance industries have already begun introducing telematics-style tracking. Programs like John Hancock’s Vitality (developed by the South African third-party company Discovery Limited), UnitedHealthcare’s Wellness Rewards, and others offer discounts, gift cards, and points for “good” behaviors.
In tandem, MAHA has been gearing up to use federal resources to promote a mass adoption of wearables. The White House strategy report to “make children healthy again,” for one, proposes linking wearable data to electronic health records. The FDA also reclassified AI-enabled wearables in January, claiming that they will not be treated as heavily regulated medical devices as long as they do not claim to diagnose or treat diseases.
Wearables do have some potential to have a positive change. In the best-case scenario, health insurance premiums would go down and Americans would live longer and more ailment-free lives. One NYC-based family medicine physician we spoke with said the people who bring wearable data to their appointments do tend to be the most health-conscious patients. But do the health conscious seek out wearables, or do wearables make users more health conscious? It’s unclear. Furthermore, the data generated are not very useful or actionable for doctors or wearers — and they are often inaccurate.
More pressingly, there is a major incentive to use consumer data to expand their profit margins. In the car industry, catchily named plans like Drivewise (Allstate), DriveEasy (Geico), and Snapshot (Progressive) extract as much data as possible from you and your car, including braking, time of day, and phone usage. Ideally, the data would be used to improve driver behavior and reduce accidents. There are some studies that point to improvement, but these are mostly for trucking fleets, and the data need to be combined with coaching and other strategies. Instead, drivers agree to opt in for lower premiums, and insurers line their pockets selling the data to third parties. The same may happen with wearable data and health insurance.
Dump five sugars in your morning coffee, skip the afternoon workout, and somewhere in a server farm in Nebraska, a spreadsheet decides you are the kind of person who dies young. Your data could be weaponized by your insurer to increase your premium and label you risky. When we are at risk, we need help, yet insurance companies and MAHA want to make the person at constant “risk” also responsible for managing that increased risk themselves.
When a hurricane hits, when cancer strikes, when a drunk driver runs a red light, no amount of personal optimization saves you. The telematics model, whether applied to your Camry or your cardiovascular system, is not a health strategy and it is not sound policy. The insurance industry has spent decades figuring out how to avoid paying for your health. Now, with an app and a MAHA press release, we may be handing the keys to the people who were already driving us into a ditch.

The DGA and IATSE may want to play footsie with Paramount over the state Attorney Generals antitrust lawsuit and hopes for a settlement. However, as the WGA has joined the charge against David Ellison‘s currently stalled $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros Discovery, a very strong arm of Hollywood labor has declared it’s time to cut the crap.
“At every step of the way, Teamsters have asked for data to show how this merger would be good for our industry, our members and domestic production,” Teamster Local 399’s Lindsay Dougherty told Deadline today. “Touting worker prosperity, without commitments, while simultaneously threatening their livelihood in the press as a bargaining chip begs the question — what is in this deal for American film and television workers?”
With Paramount leaks threatening to leave California if Golden State AG Ro Bonta and others don’t strike a deal by October 1 clearly in mind the plain speaking Dougherty added: “Fast-tracking corporate greed often lends to the creative and skilled workforce losing. Stop playing games and show us more of your commitment to the workforce.”
Watch on Deadline
While MAGA friendly Ellison and other Paramount brass have indicted everything’s “on the table,” for better or worst, the hard fact is a trial on the AGs’ action has been set for spring 2027. Rashford, Mainoo & transfers - Carrick calls for more signings
- Published
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick is determined to keep pushing to improve his squad this summer.
Carrick is about to begin his first full Premier League campaign in charge at Old Trafford.
He is acutely aware of the responsibilities that come with being the public face of such a worldwide institution, which he says it is a "privilege" to lead.
However, it also means having to address thorny issues with the media, which currently include a perceived lack of signings.
Carrick says he is delighted with United's business so far – they have spent £83m to sign Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, with the out-of-contract Karl Darlow also joining as back-up goalkeeper.
However, with weaknesses at left-back and in central midfield, as they prepare for a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick knows the work cannot stop now.
Because in a summer where his club missed out on key targets such as Elliot Anderson and Matheus Fernandes because they refused to match rival offers and are spending less than newly promoted Ipswich and Coventry, Carrick knows more transfer business needs to be done despite a desire to avoid the costly mistakes of the past.
"We want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that," he said.
"Money's money, I get that. We feel like we have to be pushing for everything we're involved in, while being realistic of what the recent history's looked like over a period of time.
"For now, we've got to make the most of it, but we've got to push every boundary we can to be able to win again, basically.
"That's the challenge."
On a personal level, Carrick had an excellent day on Thursday as his daughter got the A-level grades she was hoping for.
He cut a relaxed figure, benefiting from a rare summer when his club have avoided draining trips further afield, instead travelling to Scandinavia for matches against Wrexham, Rosenborg, Atletico Madrid and Paris St-Germain, before facing Leeds in Dublin.
"I love the position I'm in," he said.
"There's the football side; the tactical, the training, putting the team together. Then there's the other side; being the face of it, leading it, trying to set the right messages, the right behaviours and right tone for what we want to look like as a football club.
"I never take anything that this position and this football club brings for granted."
Can Carrick get the best out of Rashford?
Carrick was given a number of opportunities to say Marcus Rashford will still be a United player when the transfer window closes on 1 September, but didn't take them.
"He's our player," he kept repeating.
It was also noticeable that in talking about the England forward, he was keen to stress Rashford was not the only player in his squad he had previously coached, managed or been a team-mate of given it has been highlighted as an area of strength in the player's reintroduction.
"It is not a unique situation at all and [we] treat him exactly like any other player," he said.
However, many supporters have not forgiven Rashford for his coolness towards United during loan spells with Aston Villa and Barcelona, where everyone expected him to be this season.
It is accepted even by those who know him there is a world of difference between the disinterested figure he became under Ruben Amorim and the fully motivated one who is widely accepted to be the best player to come through the club's academy since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
Ironically, Rashford's return to United colours is likely to be against Amorim's AC Milan in Wroclaw, Poland, on Saturday.
Carrick feels the 28-year-old still has a lot to offer.
"Football's got different directions," he said. "You've got to manage through the states to have a career for 10 or 15 years. It's never going to be smooth sailing.
"But you've got to keep moving forward. If you keep looking back too much, it doesn't do anyone any favours.
"It's been good to have Marcus around this week. He's our player. He's a good player, and he gives us something a little bit different."
World Cup wasn't a wasted trip for Mainoo - Carrick
Rashford was not the only England player to return to the United fold on Sunday evening.
Kobbie Mainoo also came back.
In a sense, it feels like back to square one for Carrick with the young midfielder.
When he took over from Amorim, after Darren Fletcher's two games in interim charge in January, he had to raise the confidence of a player of undoubted talent who had been virtually ignored by his boss.
At least Mainoo did come on as a substitute for Amorim in the Premier League last season. He didn't even do that for Thomas Tuchel's World Cup squad, even though it seemed England were crying out for his ball retaining abilities in the latter stages of the competition.
Carrick knows how Mainoo feels. He was similarly overlooked by Fabio Capello during the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.
Carrick spoke to Mainoo "through the World Cup" and says he has been "in great spirits" this week.
"I spoke to him all the way through the World Cup, not loads, but little bits," he said.
"It's challenging. From the outside we all see the glitz, the glamour and all the positive sides of football.
"But players are human beings. We all have our ups and downs. It's important we support each other.
"It was a good experience for Kobbie. It's a World Cup and that is a big step.
"He's still such a young man and he's achieved so much, so quickly. To be at the stage he's at is an achievement."

Thomas's phone alarm buzzes at 9:30 pm -- it's time for the aspiring bodybuilder to start injecting himself in the stomach with several banned peptides.
He takes vials from his refrigerator of GHK-Cu, which he tells AFP will give him "beautiful skin", and Retatrutide, which will help him "feel less hungry".
After adding a liquid to reconstitute the synthetic peptides, he disinfects the syringes and shoots both into his lower abdomen.
Thomas, whose name has been changed, takes GHK-Cu daily and Retatrutide three times a week.
"It takes a little organisation, but it's become a routine," said Thomas, who goes to the gym almost every day.
He is one of a growing number of people attempting to "optimise" themselves by using peptides, a class of substances being widely promoted online by influencers, celebrities and the wellness industry.
Viral social media posts claim peptides can offer a range of seemingly miraculous benefits including glowing skin, stronger muscles, deeper sleep, a more alert mind -- and even provide an avenue to prevent ageing.
However experts warn there is little evidence to support these claims, and that because these peptides have not been studied properly, they can pose serious health risks.
That is why these peptides remain banned in many countries, including in France where Thomas lives.
In the United States, however, a panel recommended loosening restrictions on a range of peptides last month.
The decision outraged many medical experts, who accused Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- an avowed fan and user of peptides -- of packing the panel with people who have strong ties to the peptide industry.
Very real health risks
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that assemble to form proteins, which are the body's building blocks.
They occur naturally in the body, helping dictate processes such as repairing tissue.
Peptides reproduced in a lab are the active ingredients in many common medications including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
However unauthorised forms of synthetic peptides sold online have increasingly been promoted by influencers and gyms promising a more effective workout.
Thomas was already using steroids when he was introduced to peptides six months ago.
Along with GHK-Cu and Retatrutide, he sometimes injects himself with Selank for help with anxiety and BPC-157, which promises to more quickly repair soft tissue such as ligaments.
Because these peptides are not authorised for sale in France, there are no official guidelines for how to use them.
In online discussion forums such as Reddit and Discord, communities of mostly men exchange advice on how much and how often they should inject themselves.
"You read the studies, you look at the lab tests, and you see all the positive effects," said Thomas, who believes that the risks are "rare and not serious".
Self-experimentation 'worthless'
However neuroscientist Armelle Rancillac at French research institute INSERM warned that knowledge on how to use these peptides remains limited because they "have often not been tested on humans".
Earlier this year, INSERM said that "no large-scale, randomised controlled clinical trial has confirmed" the promised benefits of peptides, warning that some pose "very real health risks".
"We are not giving research enough time to prove its worth," Rancillac emphasised, adding that" scientifically worthless" accounts of self-experimentation were being given too much credence.
Numerous nations have reported people being hospitalised after using peptides. In June, Australia's government reported six cases of acute liver injury linked to products labelled Retatrutide.
It is difficult to determine how many people are using peptides, but the recent increase to exposure is enough to "raise alarm", Fabien Ohl, a sports sociologist at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland, told AFP.
Ohl criticised the "biological view" being pushed online that the human body is "capital" to be exploited by taking chemical substances to improve one's physical appearance.
For example, one website selling peptides promised to provide "the chemical architecture for those seeking absolute biological optimisation".
Self-proclaimed experts online also sell advice vowing to help men "optimise" their physique.
Ohl criticised this view of masculinity as problematic, warning it normalised an idea of "the biological male who is potentially more violent and aggressive".

Feel so busy you don't even realize you're busy? Try doing a time audit
A few years ago, Niro Feliciano didn't even have the time to grasp how busy she was. The mom of four was taking on more writing and speaking gigs on top of her work as a psychotherapist and a licensed clinical social worker.
Life Kit
Feeling short on time? Do a time audit
"I remember sitting in my office. I had done eight sessions, several with adolescents. And I said, 'When was the last time I spent 45 minutes listening to one of my kids?'" she says.
She realized that how she wanted to spend her time and how she was really spending it "were very much misaligned," she says. "I did not see enough of a reflection of things that brought me joy and contentment."
If your day leaves you no room to enjoy what matters, reevaluate where your time is going, says Feliciano, author of two self-help books, including This Book Won't Make You Happy: Eight Keys to Finding True Contentment.
Feliciano asks many of her own clients to do this, especially those who feel like they're on a "hamster wheel and can never catch up," she says. "Oftentimes, the things that are most important to them don't have much of a place in their day-to-day schedule."
To regain control of your time — and your life — try these exercises from Feliciano.
Do a time audit
Make a list of the people and the activities that are the most important to you. It might be loved ones like your partner, your kids or your bestie, and hobbies like reading, working out or video-chatting with your long-distance friends.
Then do a time inventory. Where is your time really going each day? Are the lists matching up? You might find that a lot of your day is spent on obligations, chores and time-sucking activities.
Then look for ways to make your lists reflect each other. Where can you carve out more space for your family? Or set aside a moment for reading?
"When your schedule begins to align with your values is when we begin to feel inner peace," she says.
Cut back on the time-wasters
To make more time, you'll need to set some boundaries, Feliciano says. "What are you doing that makes you feel resentful, depleted, exhausted?" And what can you do to limit yourself from those activities?
Feliciano found that she was spending a lot of unnecessary time scrolling on social media — but that wasn't on her list of priorities, so she cut back.
You may need to communicate with other people that you are taking a break. For example, you might tell your friend (who's a bit of an energy vampire) that you're pausing for a bit on weekly trivia.
Those who have your best interests in mind will understand. "The only people who will push back on your healthy boundaries are the people who benefited from you not having them," Feliciano says.
Don't overlook where you can gain time. Feliciano often has this conversation with mothers, "because they are doing so much for their children and partners," she says. Enlist family members' help with everyday tasks and chores. "That's good for everyone on board."
Learn to exist in the open space you've created
Be purposeful with your newfound time, Feliciano says. Do something joyful. Catch up with an old friend. Start that project you've been meaning to get to. "If we think about those things prior to that moment, we'll know how to fill it," she says.
Get comfortable with being bored. "Do you have a few minutes where you can just be still and rest your body? Even doing nothing is OK," she says.
And don't forget: The impulse to be busier and busier can leave you in endless pursuit. "When your value and identity lie in acquisition and accomplishment, you will constantly be pursuing it," she says. "It's a cycle that you're constantly going to be chasing unless you choose to get off it."

Today, Instagram unveiled a refresh of its wordmark, accompanied by the usual bland corporate platitudes these kinds of announcements are always packaged with.
Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri called it “leaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that’s always made it Instagram.”
Sure, Adam. Simplicity and craft are definitely what everyone thinks of when Instagram comes to mind.
I might be more inclined to think ruthless algorithmic capture, relentless influencer hype cycles, and don’t forget mining every last gram of your personal data to be packaged and repackaged and sold.
Potato, potahto.
Still, it’s been 10 years since the wordmark was updated, and in the current fruit fly life cycle of frenzied tech rebirths, that’s almost staid. This kind of housekeeping for a brand isn’t something I would normally remark on.
But I had two thoughts when I looked at the new text. The first is the one we probably all had, “Why does it say Instagzam?”
It got the job done. Was it dated? Yeah, probably. The new version definitely feels more modern. But that doesn't mean I think it's actually successful.

Students of a state-run school blocked a road for nearly seven hours on Thursday in Jharkhand's Garhwa district to protest the transfer of their headmaster, officials said.
Garhwa District Education Officer (DEO) Jagarnath Lohra said Malay Kumar Singh had been serving as headmaster on deputation at the Kandi Plus-2 High School for nearly two months.
On August 12, Singh was directed to report back to his parent institution, Lawahi Kala High School in Dandai block of the district, he said.
"The students did not want the headmaster to leave the school and staged a protest. Considering their demand, the department has decided not to send him back to his parent institution and allow him to continue serving on deputation at the Kandi Plus-2 High School," Lohra told PTI.
The students ended their protest after receiving the assurance, he said.
Garhwa SP Ashutosh Shekhar said the students initially demonstrated near the school premises, carrying banners and posters demanding that the headmaster be retained.
They later blocked the Kandi-Bhawnathpur Main Road, disrupting traffic for several hours, he said.
"There are also allegations that some students vandalised nearby shops, but no case had been registered as police had not received any complaint," he said.

India’s festive shopping journey is becoming less linear with every season, and Snapchat is betting that this transition can help deepen its advertising business in the country and give a major push to its commerce ambitions. New research by GWI and Snapchat suggests that Gen Z’s purchase journey has moved from discovery to social validation before conversion. While 70% of Gen Z consumers say creator content helps them discover products, 76% say instant feedback from trusted people makes them more confident about purchase decisions, while 63% share products with friends or family before buying. That shift is particularly relevant for Snapchat, whose proposition is built around communication between close friends and family rather than just passive content consumption. Among its daily Gen Z users, 75% say they chat with friends on Snapchat about purchases while an item is in their basket, while 67% say the platform helps them feel more confident about festive purchase decisions. For Snap India, however, the opportunity goes beyond festive advertising. The company claims a 10X increase in advertisers over the past two years and 3X growth in consistent advertiser spend, with the advertiser base expanding from largely new-age, online-first companies to traditional, offline and newer brands. The bigger question is whether Snapchat can convert its strong Gen Z positioning and growing advertiser base into a materially larger advertising business in India, particularly as marketers increasingly demand measurable performance rather than just reach. From Gen Z Awareness To The Purchase Decision For years, Snapchat’s India pitch to advertisers was relatively straightforward: Generation Z is here, so brands targeting Gen Z should be here too. That pitch appears to be evolving. The GWI-Snapchat research suggests that discovery is only the first stage of the consumer journey. Four in 10 Gen Z consumers actively seek opinions or advice before purchasing, while 63% share products with friends or family before making a purchase. Snap is therefore positioning itself closer to the point where consideration happens. “The place where we differentiate and where we stand out from other platforms is our attention,” said Yagnesh Ravi, lead of ad solutions, Snap India. Ravi points to Snap’s camera-first interface, communication between close friends and immersive advertising formats as differentiators. He cited Snap research showing that adding Snapchat to a media mix increased Gen Z attention scores by 22%. The challenge, however, is turning that attention into incremental advertising budgets. Marketers already have established channels across Meta, YouTube, Google and, increasingly, retail media networks. High engagement alone may not be enough to shift budgets unless Snapchat can demonstrate that its environment generates stronger consideration, conversion or return on ad spend. That is where the platform’s growing emphasis on performance advertising becomes important. Snap does not disclose an India-specific split between brand and performance advertising. Ravi, however, pointed to a global figure, where 75% of advertising was performance-led, while clarifying that the company does not provide the corresponding India numbers. The Broadening Advertiser Base Snap’s biggest India advertising change may be the composition of its advertiser base. Its advertiser numbers have grown 10X in two years, while consistent spending has grown 3X. Initially, the focus was more heavily tilted towards larger and online-first brands. Over the past 18 months, according to the company, more advertisers across sizes and categories have entered the ecosystem. “Two to three years ago, there was a lot of ‘why Snap’. Now the question is ‘how do I get my Snap marketing in place?’” Ravi said. Traditional FMCG and mass-market brands, for instance, can use Snap primarily to maximise reach among Gen Z, while premium brands can go deeper into affluent cohorts. But the expansion also raises a harder question: how much of this advertiser growth is translating into meaningful revenue scale? Snap has more than 250 Mn users in India, but user scale does not automatically translate into monetisation. To bridge this gap, Snap has been investing in a local team and expanding its advertising suite to accelerate monetisation. “We’re building for Rakhi, we’re building for Karwa Chauth, Onam to Diwali,” he added. The festive research reinforces why that localisation matters. Nearly four in 10 Gen Z consumers begin planning Diwali purchases more than a month in advance, while 70% view the festive season as multiple celebrations rather than a single shopping moment. For Snap, this creates a longer advertising window. But it also means marketers will expect the platform to deliver measurable outcomes throughout the funnel, not simply seasonal visibility. AI Making Snap’s Ad Business More Efficient Like virtually every major digital advertising platform, Snap is pushing AI deeper into its advertising stack. The company has built its Smart Campaign Solutions, which automate areas such as bidding, budgets, creatives and formats. It has also introduced integrations with AI platforms and is using generative AI more extensively within creative products. The strategy has two distinct objectives: improve advertiser efficiency and make advertising itself more engaging. “One is on efficiency and how do you improve performance, and then the other side is on creative delight,” Ravi said. Snap’s AI-powered creative push includes features such as AI Lenses and AI Sponsored Snaps. Ravi cited a campaign with Amazon Prime Video that allowed users to imagine themselves as characters from its shows. This could become particularly important as advertisers increasingly demand more creative variations, faster campaign deployment and better optimisation. But there is still a gap between AI capability and demonstrated economic impact. Ravi did not provide specific India-level metrics on how much AI has improved advertiser ROI or reduced campaign management costs. That leaves a key question for Snap: as AI becomes table stakes across digital advertising, will these tools create a genuine competitive advantage or simply bring Snapchat closer to the capabilities advertisers already expect elsewhere? From Sponsored Snaps To Chat Perhaps the most interesting part of Snap’s advertising strategy is its attempt to monetise the conversation itself. The GWI research shows why. Among daily active users, 43% have asked friends for shopping opinions on Snapchat, while 42% have sent a Snap to a friend specifically to ask for an opinion while shopping. That behaviour gives Snapchat an opportunity that traditional feed-based platforms may find harder to replicate: becoming part of the consumer’s purchase-validation loop. Ravi believes Chat could eventually become a meaningful advertising and commerce surface as users increasingly move conversations into close circles. Sponsored Snaps, according to Ravi, are already delivering strong results across both brand and performance objectives, with the format designed to blend naturally into the platform experience. This is where Snapchat’s festive strategy and its broader India monetisation ambitions converge. The platform is no longer simply arguing that Gen Z discovers products on Snapchat. It wants to establish that Gen Z discusses, validates and ultimately decides what to buy there. The opportunity is significant, but so is the execution challenge. Gen Z’s growing reliance on trusted circles may give Snapchat a differentiated advertising environment, but advertisers will ultimately judge the platform on incremental reach, conversion and ROI. For Snap India, the next phase is therefore less about proving that Gen Z uses Snapchat. That case appears increasingly settled. The harder task is proving that Gen Z attention, conversations and purchase intent can become a large, measurable and repeatable advertising business.

New research has revealed that an upcoming real estate development is expected to be home to the world's closest residential complex to a Disney theme park.
Disney isn’t famous for pioneering in real estate but in fact this has been at the heart of its theme park strategy for decades. The first Disneyland in California was such a success when it opened in 1955 that a string of motels and restaurants sprung up next to it spoiling the immaculate theming of the resort. To prevent a repeat of this when he was developing Disney World in Orlando in the 1960s, Walt Disney bought the land there using shell companies with cryptic names such as Tomahawk Properties and M.T. Lott Co.
If he had bought the land directly, the owners might have asked for more money safe in the knowledge that the buyer could afford it. Instead, Walt paid the going rate and word didn't get out that he was behind it until he had snapped up multiple plots spanning a massive 43 square miles. In order to control the standards there, Disney needed to have municipal governance which required actual residents in the area. As a result, tiny municipalities were established near to the fairytale-themed Magic Kingdom park. These groups of houses stand to this day and are reportedly reserved for long-term Disney employees. That's just the start of the story.
Walt was so fascinated by town planning that he commissioned the construction of an experimental city at heart of Disney World with plans for 20,000 residents who would be ferried around by monorails whilst road traffic was kept underground in order to protect pedestrians.
The plan died along with Walt in 1966 and instead Disney built a science-inspired theme park in Orlando which is known as Epcot in a nod to its predecessor as it stands for Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow. Elements of the original plans were revisited in the early 1990s when Disney developed Celebration, a quintessentially-American master-planned community which borders Disney World.
Since then, an even more exclusive gated community called Golden Oak has also sprung up on the sprawling site. Many of the houses there have Disney-themed rooms and have sold for as much as $23 million.
Disney's first international outpost came in 1983 in Tokyo where land had to be reclaimed from the sea to build the resort. Although it doesn't have as much space as Disney World in Orlando, it still spans a massive 494 acres which is quite a luxury given that it is less than 10 miles from the center of one of the most densely-populated cities on earth.
Tokyo Disney Resort was followed in 1992 by Disneyland Paris where the real estate division arose almost out of necessity. Its origin dates back decades before the theme park complex opened.
At the instigation of the late president Charles de Gaulle, new towns began to emerge in France at the end of the 1960s as a counter to haphazard urban growth. One was due to be built on a vast plot of land to the east of Paris and the five existing villages there were meant to be integrated into it. The plan was put on ice following the 1973 oil crisis but it wasn't forgotten.
In the 1980s Disney began negotiating with the French government about building a Parisian theme park and one of its objectives was to acquire far more land than the space on which its theme parks would sit. Disney needed the land so that it could maintain its meticulous standards throughout the entire resort and prevent the surrounding fantasy environment from being spoiled.
Accordingly, Disney requested a plot of land almost a fifth the size of Paris and although it got what what it wanted, it came with a catch. The government agreed to sell Disney the land provided that the majority of it was developed in accordance with its own vision. Part of this involved the development of the Val d'Europe new town spanning the existing villages including Chessy, the home of Disneyland Paris itself which is why the rail station at the park gates is called Marne-la-Vallée – Chessy.
The colossal cost of Disney's Parisian resort led to it putting the development of new international resorts on hold for more than a decade until Hong Kong Disneyland opened in 2005. As Disney co-owns the resort with the government, it was allocated a prime position on a neglected island just 15 miles from the city center giving it similar characteristics to its counterpart in Tokyo. Likewise, the Chinese government owns Shanghai Disney Resort with the media giant which helped it to snag a prized spot of 963 acres less than 20 miles from the city center.
A Whole New World
Disney's seventh resort will be a whole new world. Not only will it feature Disney's first waterfront theme park, it will also be integrated into a mixed-use destination which has already been developed. It is coming to Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and will be located on the man-made Yas Island which already features perhaps the widest range of attractions of any entertainment complex worldwide. They include a marina, an arena, a mega mall with 370 shops, deluxe hotels, beaches, a race circuit, CLYMB – the world's tallest indoor climbing wall – and a golf course which hosts a round of the PGA European Tour. They are all within walking distance of four world-class theme parks – Warner Bros. World, SeaWorld, Ferrari World and Yas Waterworld.
Yas Island is run by government-backed leisure operator Miral which, in just the past 15 years, has become the world’s leading theme park manager alongside Disney and Universal. Miral licenses the Intellectual Property for its its theme parks which it owns and operates. Thanks to its deep pockets, Miral cuts no corners and ensures that each of its attractions outdoes its predecessors. As this report explained, this strategy ensures that guests keep on returning which boosts Abu Dhabi's tourism revenues and reduces its reliance on income from its declining fossil fuel reserves.
Miral's trailblazing chief executive Mohamed Al Zaabi is the driving force behind Abu Dhabi's spellbinding theme park strategy. The INSEAD-educated industry veteran began his career in business working for the UAE government before joining Miral in 2015 where he has cast a powerful spell.
Thanks to his magic touch, there were more than 38 million visits to Yas Island in 2024 and this upward trend continued in 2025 as the destination had a record-breaking summer with a 15% year-on-year increase in visits and an average occupancy rate of 85% in its hotels. Guests came from far and wide with 31% growth from China, 86% from Russia and 47% from the United Kingdom, partly driven by Yas Island’s inaugural ad campaign in London as I reported in the City A.M. newspaper.
Such is the strength of Yas Island’s appeal that visitors continued to stream through its turnstiles this year despite the UAE being in the grip of a regional war. As this report explained, soon after the war began, Miral seized the moment and put annual passes back on sale to boost local tourism and compensate for international airlines canceling flights to the region. The masterstroke led to Yas Island's parks being packed with guests during the peak of the conflict. Indeed, they were so busy that when Yas Waterworld launched a new slide tower in April it reached capacity by early afternoon on opening day. It didn't stop there.
During a long weekend at the end of May, attendance at the parks and CLYMB was 32% higher than last year with the on-site hotels hitting 92% occupancy at an average daily rate of $347.99 (AED1,278). In turn, this helped to drive Abu Dhabi to the highest levels of hotel occupancy in the UAE in the first half of the year.
"All these numbers reflect the success of Yas Island’s vision and what we are building on Yas Island. Therefore, we are adding more attractions, more experiences, more rooms," Al Zaabi told me. Just last month a new DC Comics attraction opened in Warner Bros. World with a cutting-edge Superman roller coaster on the way in 2028 followed by a Harry Potter land, the Disney park and an offshoot of the Las Vegas Sphere.
The Magic Formula
Miral is only responsible for part of the magic formula behind these sparkling results. The high standards across Yas Island aren't limited to the theme parks but also its immaculate public areas. Manicured grass verges line the sidewalk, murals adorn the walls of apartment blocks and intricate sculptures stand at the entrances of buildings, including one which looks like a row of steel columns from one angle but from another it seems to show six falcons in flight. This attention to detail is thanks to Aldar Properties, arguably the world's finest real estate developer.
Established in 2004, Aldar made its name developing the residential communities, commercial spaces and infrastructure on Yas Island along with the nearby cultural district of Saadiyat Island. Aldar works hand-in-hand with Miral to ensure that new housing projects, pedestrian walkways and internal road networks align seamlessly with the megaprojects on Yas Island. It has $14.2 billion (AED52 billion) of assets under management including 146,000 residential units which are anything but ordinary. Its Ansam residential blocks have a Mediterranean style with cream-colored walls and curved terracotta tiles on the roofs. In contrast, Water's Edge has white-washed walls with colorful murals on the end of the blocks which are built around a canal network.
Proving that it can apply its skills to different styles, Aldar was also behind the iconic W Hotel which sits in the middle of the island and looks like a beached spaceship with its cocoon-like shell formed from 5,800 diamond-shaped glass panels. LED lights are embedded in them enabling messages and shapes to stream across the structure at night. The exterior of Disney's Tron roller coaster ride in Orlando appears to have been inspired by it and that's far from the only similarity between the two resorts.
With its cream-colored walls, corrugated terracotta tiles, exposed wooden rafters and wrought iron chandeliers, the Spanish-style clubhouse at the Yas Links golf course closely resembles the summerhouse at Golden Oak. Fittingly, the clubhouse was the site of a spectacular drone show which celebrated the announcement of Disneyland Abu Dhabi and set a new record as this report revealed.
These exacting standards are driven by Aldar's chairman Mohamed Al Mubarak, who is also chairman of Miral and Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT). A graduate of Northeastern University in Boston, Al Mubarak is a theme park fanatic as he explained to this author in an interview at the opening of Warner Bros. World in 2018. "Theme parks are not just there for kids," he said. "Every adult is a kid inside, they just have to find them, and a place like Warner Bros Abu Dhabi is an easy place for that to be found."
Al Mubarak is one of Abu Dhabi’s most prominent business figures having turned the city into a global cultural powerhouse. As I reported in amusement industry title Blooloop, his pioneering approach brought the Louvre, the Natural History Museum and a National Museum to Saadiyat Island with a Guggenheim on the way. It helped to get the Disney deal across the line with its former chief executive Bob Iger telling CNBC last year that "when you consider Abu Dhabi, you have to appreciate the fact that they have shown a great interest in arts and creativity."
Although the precise location of the Disney park has yet to be officially announced, it is an open secret. At last year’s Global Rail Transport Infrastructure Exhibition and Conference, the government-owned Abu Dhabi Transport Company (ADT) unveiled a map, which can be seen here, showing that the Disney park will be located on a beach in the north of Yas Island.
This was confirmed by the official Visit Abu Dhabi website which temporarily revealed the north beach location in September last year as this report by Arabian Gulf Business Insight (AGBI) explained. Iger himself even confirmed it when he shared two photos on Instagram in January with the caption "Walking the site of what will one day be Disneyland Abu Dhabi! Lots of work ahead, but all very exciting!"
The National newspaper tallied landmarks in the photos with the north beach site which happens to be the largest area of clear land on the coast of Yas Island so it makes sense for the waterfront park to be located there.
Last month Aldar announced that the site will be bordered by the new 600,000 square meter $1.6 billion (AED6 billion) Yas Point waterfront development which will feature around 1,600 residences for 5,000 residents as well as a five-star resort hotel, an international school, retail and dining outlets. The first phase, called The Canopies, features 592 apartments which will all be within walking distance of a 700-meter promenade along with cycling routes, gardens and three public parks.
Like Disney’s upcoming residential communities in North Carolina and Rancho Mirage, California, The Canopies will have a central clubhouse for residents. It even has the Disney-esque name of The Canopy Club while The Clearing is an outdoor pavilion for yoga and The Afterglow is an immersive garden experience with illuminated installations that come alive at dusk.
Fireworks On The Horizon
Handover of The Canopies is expected for 2030 with the Disney park expected to open after that. It will be a dream ticket for residents as can be seen in this new Aldar advert for Yas Point which shows fireworks erupting in the sky from just beyond the promenade. It appears to be the first piece of official concept art of the Disney park which has been released since two deliberately vague drawings were distributed at the announcement of the resort in May last year. If so, It seems to clear up one of the biggest questions that fans have had about its flagship park.
Saying that Abu Dhabi has a hot climate is somewhat of an understatement. Often the heat billows from all angles like it is coming from a huge hairdryer and the sidewalk can get so hot that it melts the soles of shoes. The air feels hotter and more humid than a bathroom after a hot shower and often you can’t even cool down with fans which spray mist as the water warms up before it hits your skin. In winter, it can reach 90 degrees and in recent weeks the mercury has surged above 110 giving it a heat index of more than 130. To put that into context, in Orlando the National Weather Service issues "excessive heat warnings" if the 'feels like' temperature passes 113 degrees.
Part of the secret to Miral's success is that, aside from Yas Waterworld, all of the Yas Island parks are indoors. Not only does this shield guests from the intense heat, it also allows the parks to be decorated with intricately-detailed scenery as it isn't open to the elements.
The two initial pieces of concept art seemed to show that the upcoming park will follow Disney’s typical format of being largely outdoors. However, Al Zaabi suggested otherwise in a revealing interview with the the Middle East's local edition of Forbes when he said "we know from our experience that an outdoor theme park would never work." It sparked suggestions from fans that an indoor setting would disrupt Disney's famous theme park sightlines – landscapes with layers of attractions in the background – and would prevent it from hosting the Mouse's trademark nightly fireworks.
It doesn't look like that from the advert which carries the caption "extraordinary lights up the night" along with the description: "no matter where you are, you'll always have the best view. A new destination is coming to the northernmost tip of Yas Island." The art doesn't say that the fireworks are at the Disney resort but none of the other parks on Yas Island have outdoor pyro displays and there are no other local shows which take place often enough to justify including them in the marketing as the main selling point. Likewise, although the art is not from Miral or Disney, it is from Aldar which is Miral's partner on Yas Island and is part-owned by the government's Mubadala Investment Company. In short, it is in the know.
The art even resembles the designs (which can be seen here) for the biggest resort at Disneyland Paris which also has water views, though they are of a lake rather than the ocean as is the case in Abu Dhabi.
More concept art is expected to be unveiled at Disney’s D23 convention this weekend. The world’s five leading theme park pundits have all expressed their hope for announcements about Abu Dhabi at the event. Drew Smith, theme park expert and content creator at Drew the Disney Dude, discussed this with FOX 35 while it was mentioned in reports by the four others – Tharin White, lead publisher of EYNTK.info, Coaster Studios’ maestro Taylor Bybee, Zach Perilstein, editor-in-chief of Boardwalk Times and Robert Niles of Theme Park Insider.
A Walk In The Park
As the park's precise location hasn't been announced yet, it's unclear where its entrance will be but if it is built near the border of Yas Point, it could enable a resident of The Canopies to step out of their apartment and be at the front gates in a matter of minutes. Given Yas Point's proximity to the site it would make it the world's closest residential complex to a Disney park as the table below shows:
The results are based on the shortest practical walking distance to a theme park in each Disney resort rather than the straight-line distance as that is often unusable. In a number of cases the straight-line distance crosses wetlands, restricted property or highways. Driving distance isn't comparable either as the routes in and out of the parks often take a winding route through parking lots and surrounding roads which are longer in some countries than others thereby distorting the results.
Windermere Cay for example is roughly a mile from the Magic Kingdom area, but more than five miles from the public entrance by a practical pedestrian route. Disney Vacation Club timeshare rooms aren't included in the results as the maximum length for a single, continuous reservation there is just 30 days. The results are based on residential complexes with properties that can be bought or rented by the public rather than individual homes because once they sell up the public has no way of accessing them. This rules out the pricey Golden Oak but even if it was included it wouldn't beat The Canopies as there isn't even a practical walking route from the development.
Although the entrance of Disney’s Abu Dhabi park may end up being further from The Canopies’ border than forecast above, it has already given a glow to the development. Aldar recently revealed that it generated $0.4 billion (AED1.5 billion) in sales during the launch of The Canopies with 84% of buyers being first time customers, 40% being UAE nationals with the remainder expats and overseas buyers.
Aldar’s supremely skilled chief financial officer Faisal Falaknaz told AGBI in October that Yas "has been doing incredibly well on the back of the Disney announcement. Land values have gone up at least 20 [or] 30 percent. So have residential prices there. We expect that momentum to continue."
Crucial to this success is Aldar’s chief commercial officer Cecilia Reinaldo who said that Disney's decision to open on Yas Island "is not just a brand milestone; it’s a strategic inflection point for the regional real estate market." It is no exaggeration.
Just five days after Disney revealed that it is coming to Yas Island, Aldar announced that it will build residences there themed to the ultra-upscale Waldorf Astoria hotel chain. The announcement was made on the pristine greens of Yas Links which is where the Waldorf Astoria residences will be located.
They were the brainchild of Dan Wakeling, Hilton's supremely skilled vice president of luxury residence development in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. He signed the Yas Island Waldorf Astoria deal with Jonathan Emery, Aldar Development's chief executive and one of the world's most experienced real estate managers.
Emery spent 19 years at British property development titan Hammerson before moving to Middle Eastern entertainment conglomerate Majid Al Futtaim in 2008. As I have reported, Majid Al Futtaim also develops master-planned residential communities and Emery grew the business from a start-up to a value of $5 billion. He repeated the trick at Aldar which he steered to three consecutive years of growth after he joined in November 2020. There was more to come.
The Waldorf Astoria residences broke records last year by becoming one of Aldar's fastest-selling properties. All 133 homes sold out within 24 hours of going on sale netting Aldar $231.4 million (AED850 million). It helped its revenue rise 47% to a record $9.2 billion (AED33.8 billion) in 2025, leaving it with a net profit of $2.4 billion (AED8.8 billion).
Even the war hasn't stopped this surge. Aldar recently announced that its revenue in the first half of this year rose 8% to $4.6 billion (AED16.8 billion) fueling an 18% increase in net profit to $1.3 billion (AED4.9 billion). Yas Point should sprinkle even more pixie dust on Aldar's bottom line in the next quarter as sales opened at the end of July. In Summary
- The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of the latest series of foldable phones showcased by Samsung, the others being the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra .
- While the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra broadly stick to more conventional form factors, the Z Fold 8 comes with a more square-ish, wider design.
- The Z Fold 8 comes with top-of-the-line hardware, but its design is what makes it perhaps the most innovative foldable we have seen for a while.
Foldable phones started out as being insanely innovative. And then proceeded to become as predictable as the unfoldables. Every year saw foldable devices that were essentially the same as their predecessors, and just like the non-foldies, were “thinner and more powerful than before.” Innovation on the foldable front seemed to be following the “retain design, improve specs, make thinner” formula seen on normal phones, with the addition of a “this time you cannot even see the crease” line!
Which is why the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes as a much-needed breath of fresh air in the foldable segment. At last there is something that’s different on the foldable front, beyond the usual slim, specs and crease conversation.
A distinct square-ish look that reminds one of pocketbooks
The Z Fold 8 brings the most basic innovations to the foldable table – it looks different and works differently. Yes, it does also come with flagship-level specs, but we do not think too many people will buy it for its spec sheet. The spec chasers with deep pockets are more likely to be attracted to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, while those on a tighter budget will not extend themselves beyond the relatively affordable Z 8 Flip. But those who want something different will go for the Z Fold 8.
While the Z Fold 8 follows the “open to get a bigger display” tradition of all foldables, it tries to hit the middle ground between the Z Flip 8 and the Z Fold 8 Ultra, attempting to blend the compactness of the Flip form factor with the productivity of the Fold 8 Ultra. It has a 5.5-inch cover display that is larger than the 4.1-inch one of the Z Flip 8 and a 7.5-inch main (internal) display that is slightly smaller than the 8-inch one on the Z Fold 8 Ultra. It, however, retains the Fold series’ quality of opening from the side rather than upwards as in the Flip.
However, unlike Galaxy Fold devices of the past – and most non-flip foldables – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is actually shorter and wider than most phones. When shut, the Galaxy Z Fold 7 is 123.9 mm tall, which makes it one of the most compact devices out there, beaten only by foldables that flip (the Z Flip 8 itself is 85.7 mm tall). But what is interesting is that at 81.9 mm (when shut), it is one of the widest devices out there – the iPhone 17 Pro Max is 78 mm wide, for comparison.
This gives the Z Fold 8 a very distinct, slightly squarish look, like one of those pocket books that we used to carry around for making quick notes. This squarish appearance was quite the rage once upon a time – Motorola used it in the Moto Charm, Blackberry used it in the aptly-named Passport – but has largely gone out of fashion. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 attempts to bring it back into our lives, with a fold in the middle.
The fold that is just the type for those who like to type
From our limited experience of it so far, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the most comfortable foldable we have used in terms of portability, usability and productivity. The reason for that is its shape. Samsung has marketed the Galaxy Z Fold 8 as one which delivers a reel-friendly 16:10 aspect ratio when shut and opens up to reveal a more book-like 3:2 aspect ratio, making it the perfect device to view content on, but we think that is only part of the appeal of the device.
The wider-than-usual 5.5-inch cover display makes typing on the Z Fold 8 actually easier than even on the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which has a larger, but narrower, 6.5-inch display. In fact, this is perhaps the best typing experience we have had on a phone for a long time, although we do feel that its form factor makes it perfect for writing on – it actually gives us those classic notepad feels.
Time to be square again?
Of course, this does result in our opening the Z8 Fold less often as compared to the Z Flip 8 and the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which makes us wonder if it is time for the square-ish form factor, but that is another story for another day. We will also write more about the entire Fold experience in our detailed review. But as of now, it is safe to state that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perhaps the most radical change we have seen in a foldable since they came into existence.
It is also the first foldable we have written about without any mention of its processor, storage, RAM, cameras, or even software. The Z Fold 8 makes all of these seem secondary to the way in which it looks and works. Actually, we do not even think we have mentioned its price either. Which is what tech really should be about. In purely tech terms, we are flipping for this fold.

In August 2026, a rumor spread on the internet that a photograph authentically showed U.S. President Donald Trump hiding in an airplane catering cart as he was being smuggled from one plane to another for security reasons.
The image circulated after the New York Times reported on Aug. 10 that, in July, Trump had to be smuggled from Air Force One onto a military jet in a catering container to leave Turkey because he faced a credible threat from Iran.
The image appeared on Facebook, Bluesky, LinkedIn and X. Anthony Scaramucci, who was the White House communications director during Trump's first administration, also posted the image from his X account on Aug. 11, saying the president was "livid" that the image became public (archived):
The image showed Trump's face peering out from behind a plane food tray in a small airplane catering cart or trolley that was open on the side.
However, the image was fake. As we outline below, the man who created it confirmed he'd made it and that it was not real.
Further, t
Further, a search on Google, DuckDuckGo and Bing turned up no credible report that this image was authentic. 
The earliest posting of this image we could identify came shortly after the New York Times article was published on Aug. 10. A Bluesky account named Matt Ortega shared the photo:
— Matt Ortega (@mattortega.com) 10 August 2026 at 21:30
The account belonged to a congressional candidate in California who lost the Democratic primary on June 2, 2026. His campaign website indicates Ortega has a long history of satirizing political content. During the 2012 presidential election, Salon identified Ortega as "the man behind Mitt Romney memes," referring to the then-Republican presidential candidate (Romney lost to former Democratic President Barack Obama).
"I made it myself. (It's not real.)," Ortega told Snopes in a Bluesky message exchange.
Details in the image suggest it was generated via artificial intelligence. First, it is implausible that a person of the president's size could easily hide in the narrow trolley. Further, while catering trolleys on airplanes have doors, they do not include curtains. The curtains on the trolley in this image resembled those that separate seats on airplanes, to distinguish first, business or economic class.
We also ran the image through the ZeroGPT AI image detector, which suggested that the image was AI-generated with 97% certainty, though AI image detectors can be unreliable.
This image was not the sole example of fabricated image making light of the story that Trump was smuggled out of Turkey in catering equipment. Snopes found other examples on X and Facebook.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated several fake images of Trump, including one that showed Trump asleep in the Oval Office of the White House, with his face on the Resolute Desk.

Jaisalmer man abducted, brutally assaulted, nose cut off: Police
The attackers allegedly broke his hands and legs and cut off his nose with a sharp-edged weapon before fleeing after villagers chased them
A 27-year-old man was allegedly abducted at gunpoint and brutally assaulted by a group of men while he was returning home with three children in his camper vehicle in Jaisalmer district on Thursday evening, police said.
The attackers allegedly broke his hands and legs and cut off his nose with a sharp-edged weapon before fleeing after villagers chased them.
Sankra SHO Ran Singh Sodha while confirming the development said that the incident took place around 7pm near the Rajgarh-Khelana border area.
“Rajgarh resident Jamal Khan, son of Farid Khan, was returning home from Bhainsda with three children when two vehicles followed him and forced him to stop.
The accused allegedly took him into their vehicle at gunpoint and abducted him,” the SHO said.

The incident came to light when some villagers passing through the area heard cries for help. Suspecting something was wrong, they followed the attackers’ vehicles. Police said the accused, fearing that they were being surrounded, allegedly dumped Jamal in an injured condition by the roadside and fled.
