Hong Kong’s university town: where’s the money and what will success look like?
Hong Kong is betting big on the Northern Metropolis with a university town as a core engine. In this third of a five-part series on the city’s five-year plan, we look at the talk of the town
Hong Kong is a city that has among the highest concentration of top universities with at least eight making it to global and regional rankings and as excitement builds over a new economic hub, a new buzz phrase has emerged in the sector – ‘university town’.
One is set to emerge in the Northern Metropolis, spanning from Ngau Tam Mei eastward to Hung Shui Kiu and the New Territories North, covering a total area of 1,000 hectares (2,471 acres) including 300 hectares of campus space.
But the experts expected to make it all happen are treading warily, asking anxious questions even as they avow commitment.
To realise this ambition of creating a hub for education, innovation, and technology, university leaders are calling for three main things: clarity on the development parameters, the timeline, and the financing model.
Most see the town as a space to potentially expand their research and development (R&D) schemes into application projects and field trials.
Beyond this consensus, they each have a wish list on what ought to be in the new town, as envisioned in the city’s inaugural five-year plan due out by the end of next month.
“We are not paying lip service. We wish to invest, alongside the government, other universities and enterprises, to build the Northern Metropolis,” said Professor Christopher Chao Yu-hang, senior vice-president for research and innovation at Polytechnic University.

It is true that a new law made it possible to obtain an abortion in Massachusetts on a physician's "professional medical judgment" after the 24th week of pregnancy. However …
… Pregnancy terminations after that point already were legal in the state in four cases: to preserve the life of the gestating person; to preserve the gestating person's physical or mental health; in case of defect or diagnosis that would result in the death of the fetus; and in the case of a "grave fetal diagnosis that indicates that the fetus is incompatible with sustained life outside of the uterus without extraordinary medical interventions."
In August 2026, a rumor spread that Massachusetts had legalized "abortion until birth," — also known as "late-term" abortion — that is, a termination after 24 weeks of pregnancy, 
The claim spread across social media, including Instagram, Facebook and X. An X post by Students for Life of America, an anti-abortion organization dedicated to recruiting and mobilizing students across the U.S., tagged Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, saying "this is evil" (archived):
The post included a video zooming in on an image of a fetus with a hand holding a syringe injecting the fetus in the heart. The video included the screenshot of an apparent post that read:
Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey just signed a law legalizing abortion up until BIRTH. Late-term abortion procedures involve injecting digoxin into a third-trimester baby's heart, inducing cardiac arrest before delivering the baby dead, as shown in this painting. This is now legal and being celebrated in Massachusetts.
This is EVIL. End late-term abortion now.
It is true that Healey signed into law a statute that enhances abortion protections after the 24-week mark, though the state's existing law already made it possible to terminate a pregnancy after that point in certain cases.
On July 22, 2026, the Massachusetts legislature passed a bill that updates "state law governing abortions after 24 weeks of pregnancy, ensuring that physicians can provide medically necessary abortion care based on their professional medical judgment."
"An abortion may be performed by a physician based upon the professional judgment of the physician," the text said.
This bill updated an existing law that made it possible to terminate a pregnancy after 24 weeks in four specific cases: to preserve the life of the gestating person; to preserve the gestating person's physical or mental health; in case of defect or diagnosis that would result in the death of the fetus; and in the case of a "grave fetal diagnosis that indicates that the fetus is incompatible with sustained life outside of the uterus without extraordinary medical interventions."
On Aug. 10, Healey signed the updated text into law, relaxing these rules. The new language says a physician's judgment is enough to make an abortion possible. Crucially, it does not leave that decision solely to the pregnant person.
Abortions after 21 weeks of pregnancy are rare and represented only 1.1% of all terminations in 2022, according to an abortion surveillance report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Meanwhile, 96% of abortions occur before 15 weeks. (In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade, the 1973 court decision that made abortion legal until viability nationwide. Therefore, pre-2022 data provides a reliable picture of abortion in the U.S.)
For further reading, Snopes has covered many claims about abortion, including the rumor that a bill in North Carolina would allow anyone to kill someone seeking an abortion.

US TerraPower, South Korea's SK Innovation sign preliminary deal on global SMR projects
SEOUL, Aug 14 : TerraPower and South Korea's SK Innovation signed on Friday a preliminary global agreement on small modular reactors (SMRs), Seoul's Industry Ministry said, opening a path for the SK Group affiliate to participate in the U.S. company's projects at home and abroad.
The agreement was signed at a meeting in Seoul between TerraPower co-founder Bill Gates, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won and Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, the ministry said.
The deal gives SK Innovation, the parent of South Korea's largest oil refiner, an opportunity to take part in development of TerraPower's SMR projects in the United States and overseas, the ministry said. It did not disclose financial terms or the scope of any investment.
TerraPower, backed by Gates, is developing its sodium-cooled Natrium reactor project in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The company received a construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission in March and is targeting commercial operation in 2031, the ministry said.
South Korea's Doosan Enerbility said on Friday it won a contract from TerraPower to manufacture key components for the reactor, including the reactor vessel, support structures and internal structures, without disclosing the value of the deal.
South Korean companies including SK and HD Hyundai have made financial investments in TerraPower and are also seeking roles in equipment supply, operations and construction for its U.S. and overseas projects, the ministry said.
The ministry said growing electricity demand from AI infrastructure and data centres was increasing global interest in SMRs, creating opportunties for Korean suppliers to enter emerging overseas supply chains.

India became independent on 15 August 1947. By 15 August, the nation will have completed 79 years of independence. However, since the day of independence itself was counted as the first Independence Day, the 2026 celebration will mark India’s 80th Independence Day.

Violence erupted near J P Chowk in Siwan as protesters clashed with police. During the confrontation, police personnel opened fire using AK-47 assault rifles and pistols.
Three youths suffered serious gunshot injuries. They were identified as 15-year-old Mohammad Arif, 21-year-old Akash Yadav and 20-year-old Bullet Kumar Gond. All three were initially admitted to Siwan Sadar Hospital before being referred to Medanta Hospital in Patna due to the severity of their injuries. Shortly after the incident, videos showing blood-soaked Akash and Arif being rushed to hospital on a rickshaw circulated widely on social media.
According to the injured and their families, none of the three was participating in the violent protest. Arif, who worked at a local shop, was allegedly shot in the neck while returning home after closing the shop because of the bandh. Akash, a resident of Rae Bareli in Uttar Pradesh, had travelled to Siwan to celebrate his birthday with his fiancée and was allegedly shot while returning after buying a cake.
Bullet Kumar Gond said he was on his way to the district magistrate’s office to obtain caste and residence certificates when he was hit by a bullet in the leg. He further alleged that police assaulted him with fibreglass batons even after he had been shot and forced him to hop on one leg to the police station. “I was left writhing in pain for about an hour before an ambulance was called,” he said.
Following the incident, a video showing a police constable firing an AK-47 rifle went viral. Bihar Police suspended constable Abhishek Kumar after the footage surfaced. In a statement issued on July 27, Siwan Police claimed the constable fired four rounds into the air after being surrounded by protesters in order to protect lives and government property. The police further claimed that no one was injured in the firing. A departmental inquiry has been ordered, and Siwan superintendent of police Puran Kumar Jha said the investigation would also examine who authorised the firing.
However, an analysis by Alt News raises questions about the police’s official account.
Alt News examined videos recorded from multiple angles by bystanders and conducted geolocation verification of the footage. The investigation found that police fired at least nine rounds from AK-47 rifles at two separate locations. In addition, two separate instances of police personnel firing pistols were captured on camera. Geolocation analysis confirmed that these videos were also recorded in Siwan during the July 25 violence.
Eight Rounds Fired in front of Siwan District Commandant’s Office
Alt News obtained videos from three different vantage points showing a police constable firing an AK-47 rifle. The footage establishes that at least eight rounds were fired by him.
By matching the shops and buildings visible in all three videos, Alt News confirmed that the footage was recorded on the road in front of the district commandant’s office in Siwan.
One Round Fired on the Road to Kagzi Mohalla, Naya Bazaar in Siwan
At a second location, Alt News identified a police officer firing at least one round from an AK-47 rifle. The organisation obtained videos of the incident recorded from two different angles. By matching the shops and buildings visible in both videos, Alt News confirmed that the footage was recorded on Kagzi Mohalla–Naya Bazaar Road, around 400 metres from the district commandant’s office in Siwan.

Policemen Firing Pistol
Alt News also verified two separate incidents of police personnel firing pistols. In one video, matching nearby buildings established that the footage was recorded on the road in front of Darbar Jama Masjid in Siwan. A second video, showing a policeman firing a pistol towards protesters, was geolocated to J P Chowk by verifying the surrounding shops and buildings.

The findings contradict the police’s official version. While Siwan Police stated that only four rounds were fired from an AK-47, Alt News verified at least nine rounds fired from AK-47 rifles at two locations, in addition to two separate instances of pistol fire. The footage also shows more than one police officer firing towards protesters.
Speaking to Scroll, injured Akash Yadav said he was shot by a policeman wielding a pistol and claimed he could identify the officer who fired at him. He also alleged that the police may have pressured him to change his statement. So far, however, action has been taken only against one constable.
Police Firing in Jehanabad on July 23
The firing in Siwan was not an isolated incident. Two days earlier, on July 23, police also opened fire while dispersing protesters in Bihar’s Jehanabad district during demonstrations over alleged irregularities in the NEET examination.
Alt News found videos of the incident recorded from two different angles, showing police personnel firing sub-machine gun carbines towards protesters. Geolocation analysis established that the footage was recorded near the Child Development Project (Anganwadi) building outside the Officers’ Colony adjacent to Jehanabad railway station.

Speaking to the media, Jehanabad district magistrate Tshering Y. Bhutia said police opened fire after protesters began pelting stones but claimed that no one was injured. He added that around 10 to 15 rounds were fired and that the situation was subsequently brought under control. Local residents, however, alleged that the number of rounds fired was significantly higher.
Political fallout
The Siwan firing quickly triggered a political storm.
Leader of Opposition in the Bihar assembly Tejashwi Yadav raised the issue on July 25, accusing the police of opening fire on students with AK-47 rifles. The following day, he visited the injured victims in hospital.
Samajwadi Party MP Akhilesh Yadav also questioned the use of AK-47 rifles against unarmed protesters, asking who had authorised the deployment of such a lethal weapon during the demonstrations in Siwan.
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi later spoke to injured Akash Yadav over the phone and assured him of assistance. During the conversation, Akash said he had been shot in the shoulder, leaving one of his hands impaired. He also told Gandhi that he had lost his mother in childhood, lived with his father and had no siblings. Referring to the Siwan incident, Rahul Gandhi alleged that the state’s response to student protests had become increasingly violent and criticised the use of AK-47 rifles against demonstrators.

Minister for Energy Resources and Law R. Nirmalkumar on Friday (August 14, 2026) claimed that the DMK and the BJP had been in a “covert” alliance earlier and had now decided to enter into a “direct” alliance.
The Minister was responding to a question during a press conference at the Secretariat in Chennai on DMK parliamentary party leader Kanimozhi meeting Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in New Delhi on Thursday (August 13).
“The DMK, which had earlier been in an indirect alliance with the BJP, has now decided to enter into a direct alliance. That was why former Minister Anitha R. Radhakrishnan said DMK MP Tiruchi Siva would soon become a Union Minister. Former DMK MP Kanimozhi N.V.N. Somu and BJP leader Vanathi Srinivasam also hinted that there were no permanent enemies or friends in politics,” he said.
When asked about Ms. Kanimozhi’s clarification that she had met Mr. Birla only to discuss the seating arrangements for the DMK MPs, Mr. Nirmalkumar questioned the rationale behind the meeting when the Lok Sabha Speaker had hosted a tea party.
Mr. Nirmalkumar accused the DMK of “surrendering” to the Union government to “protect its ill-gotten wealth.” He said the DMK had decided to do now what it had done in 2001 by forming an alliance with the BJP and giving the BJP “a recognition” in Tamil Nadu.
He said although the DMK had voted in favour of the resolution against delimitation in the Assembly, the party had not so far explicitly said that it would vote against the proposed Delimitation Bill when it was introduced in Parliament.
‘Investments high due to transparency’
Responding to a question on investments worth ₹1 lakh crore coming to Tamil Nadu in the 100 days of the TVK-led government, Mr. Nirmalkumar said all these companies had already been waiting to invest in Tamil Nadu.
During the previous DMK regime, though Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) were publicly signed, a “behind-the-screen MoU had to be entered with the family,” he alleged. Because of this, many companies were reluctant to invest in the State. Now, they are coming forward to invest because of transparency in governance, he said.
Mr. Nirmalkumar said the Southern Zonal Council meeting was expected to be held in Mamallapuram next week. The official schedule had not yet been released and arrangements for the meeting were under way, he said.

Turns out, AI agents may not be great team players.
In Anthropic's new research, published on Thursday, the AI lab said that AI agents being given the same task but with incompatible goals often threw a wrench in each other's work on purpose.
In the test, each AI model was given a software engineering task — rewriting a Python backend in another programming language, but they were given contradictory objectives. What ensued was a "multiagent turf war," the lab said.
"All of the models we tested quickly assumed that others were purposefully impeding their work, and began to sabotage others while protecting their own contributions," Anthropic wrote. "In fact, they sabotaged others with increasingly aggressive, self-replicating malware."
For example, they tried to disable each other's accounts, wrote scripts that found and killed competing processes, and deployed malicious code disguised as belonging to another agent, the lab wrote. The AI models being tested in this case were Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.8, Mythos Preview, and Mythos 5.
Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 were the most combative, settling about 60% of their runs by force instead of truces or passivity.
However, in some test runs, the models managed to communicate their goals and coordinate, Anthropic wrote.
"In many of these successful episodes, they write commit messages or markdown files apologizing for malicious behavior and coordinate a truce," it wrote. "They clean up their malicious code, clarify the nature of the conflict, and ask for a human to intervene."
The lab concluded that "coordination doesn't naturally emerge from stronger intelligence" and that work is needed to create environments that exert social pressures on agents to align with one another.
Anthropic's new research comes as AI agents increasingly demonstrate their ability to go rogue and perform autonomous, malicious actions.
Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta all self-reported that their AI agents had hacked vulnerabilities in third-party websites during cybersecurity tests, the most significant of which was the July hacking of open-source platform Hugging Face by an OpenAI agent.
Anthropic's research is timely, as businesses from startups to Big Tech scale up their AI agent workforces to increase productivity and reduce labor costs.

Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian to travel to Delhi for BRICS Summit
The visit assumes significance as India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit under its 2026 chairship.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will travel to New Delhi to attend the upcoming BRICS Summit, Iranian sources said on Friday.
Pezeshkian's participation in the summit is scheduled to be held in the national capital in September.
The visit assumes significance as India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit under its 2026 chairship. The summit will be held under India's theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability". India assumed the BRICS chairship from Brazil at the beginning of 2026.
In October 2024, Pezeshkian met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, where the two leaders discussed bilateral and regional issues.
Iran became a full member of BRICS in 2024, along with Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates. Indonesia joined the grouping in 2025, taking the total number of full members to 11.
Earlier in June, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrived in India to attend the BRICS Foreign Ministers' Meeting.
Addressing a press conference in the national capital following the meeting, Araghchi highlighted New Delhi's growing influence as a global peacemaker and asserted that India can play a "greater role" in de-escalating the volatile situation in West Asia. Araghchi made it clear that Tehran sees no future in armed conflict.
He stated that there is no military solution to the current crisis and that a "negotiated settlement" remains the only viable path forward.
Underscoring Tehran's openness to Indian mediation, he remarked, "We will welcome any constructive role by India."
Araghchi also held talks with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar where he affirmed that friendly nations can rely on Iran for commercial security.
Araghchi clarified that Iran will always carry out its historical duty as protector of security in Hormuz.
In a post on X, he said, "In fruitful engagement with my host External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, discussed regional developments and clarified that Iran will always carry out historical duty as protector of security in Hormuz. Iran is a reliable partner of all friendly nations, who can rely on safety of commerce."
Meanwhile, the Iranian government said in a post on X, "FM Seyyed Abbas Araghchi delivers Iran's statement at the BRICS Foreign Ministers' Meeting in India. He highlighted the importance of breaking Western hegemony and ensuring that international institutions remain free from political manipulation."
The developments come as West Asia remains locked in a cold, precarious stalemate amid the ongoing hostilities following the eruption of conflict on February 28, which pitted the combined forces of the United States and Israel against Iran. (ANI)

Jarrod Bowen exclusive: West Ham captain on his decision to remain with the Hammers after relegation from the Premier League
Jarrod Bowen on staying at West Ham in the Championship, missing out on the World Cup, promotion by any means and more; watch the full feature in the build-up to Burnley vs West Ham, live on Sky Sports Football and Main Event from 4pm on Sunday
Friday 14 August 2026 09:52, UK
When West Ham were relegated from the Premier League after 15 years back in May, it seemed inevitable Jarrod Bowen would not be there to join them as they returned to the Sky Bet Championship.
The Hammers captain had done all he could to try and keep them up; he had started every game and played the entirety of all but two, scoring nine goals and providing 11 assists.
Speculation about where his future might lie was rife. After six-and-a-half seasons in the top flight, could he really return to the second tier and pass up the potential opportunity to play European football again?

That question was answered emphatically on July 17 when Bowen adjusted his current deal to ensure he is committed to the club for 2026/27, though the length of the contract remains the same, expiring in 2030.
West Ham lost key players Mateus Fernandes and Crysencio Summerville this summer, but their talisman remains to spearhead the bid for an immediate return to the Premier League.
'No one needed to sell this club to me'
"I was asked about my future after we were relegated and it was about making the right decision for myself," the 29-year-old tells Sky Sports.
"I thought of it as what's going to be the biggest 'what if?' when I retire? There's going to be 'what ifs' whatever you do, but it was going to be that one that would nag away at me for years and years to come.
"I knew I had to give it a go to get this club back into the Premier League. That was the overriding factor.
"There were different talks, there were different chances of me leaving, so it wasn't a decision that was made overnight. It was something I had to sit down and think about for myself because football is so intense and full-on week in, week out.
"I'm sure there's lots being said about decisions, but it's about me, it's about what I want, what I think's best for my career."
Bowen visited Daniel Kretinsky - West Ham's largest shareholder - in Prague over the summer. "No one needs to sell the club to me. It was just an honest conversation about what we want to do as a club moving forward," Bowen says.
He insists his wife Dani Dyer and father-in-law Danny Dyer - both diehard West Ham fans - did not influence his decision either. "They are never going to be in my ear saying 'I think you should stay or I think you should go'."
"I've come on leaps and bounds as a person and a player since I've been here," he adds.
"I just love playing football, scoring goals and working hard for the team all the time. The fans have felt a connection to me, I've felt a connection to the fans and it's just been right. That's the most important thing.
"Sometimes, things can feel forced and not real, but for me everything has felt real. We've had some really great moments and I've loved every minute."
'I felt like I deserved to be in England's World Cup squad'
Bowen's form throughout 2025/26 was electric. In 42 games in all competitions, he scored 11 goals and provided 12 assists, averaging one goal involvement every other game.
Thomas Tuchel was aware and, in his first 12 games in charge of England, he played Bowen on eight occasions.
But when the squad for the 2026 World Cup was announced on May 22, Bowen's name was missing from the list.
"Don't get me wrong, it was difficult. OK, we got relegated, but as an individual, I felt like I contributed well. We didn't do well and maybe that went against me," he continued.
"It was difficult to watch to begin with because I felt like I deserved to be there. Anyone in the same situation would be saying the same thing.
"That weekend was the worst a footballer could have in terms of missing out on the England squad on the Friday, then getting relegated on Sunday. It was a very tough weekend, but I'm stood here fit, healthy and ready to go again for another season.
"Even if I'd gone to the World Cup, I would've been ready. Over the years, touch wood, I've been lucky with injuries. I look after myself well, try and do the right things, try to get the right balance of training and then having my time with my family."
'As long as we get promoted, I don't care how we do it'
Bowen may have been a consistent performer at the top level for many years now, but he's no stranger to the division he's about to play in.
Before the move to West Ham, he spent two-and-a-half seasons in the Championship with Hull, scoring 52 goals and providing 12 assists in 117 games.
"I've experienced the Championship and it's such a competitive league. I remember when I was at Hull, we were doing well in the league and you'd go to a side bottom of the league and they turn you over. It's one of the toughest leagues to get out of because it's so demanding, so physical.
"What we need to do as a team is have that winning mentality, understanding what it takes to win games. We have a manager who's been with the squad for nearly a year, who understands the club, who understands the fans and how it works.
"We've got a real togetherness as a group and that's an important thing. We've had a lot of change in the last two or three years, with managers and players, which can happen, but sticking with the manager we had from last season will really stand us in good stead."
Bowen isn't set on winning the league or going up automatically. Just going straight back up, by any means, will do.
"The worst thing I think you can do as a club is try and walk into this league and think 'we're the biggest side, we're going to go straight up'. It doesn't happen like that. It's not as easy and just turning up and thinking 'we're better, we're going to win'. That's nowhere near the case.
"You're playing Saturday-Tuesday, you're not going to play at your best every single week and you have to win in different kinds of ways. You just have to go again, go again, go again and that's got to be the mindset of us as a group.
"Of course we want to be dominant and assert our dominance in this league, but we have to earn the right to do that as well. We have to respect the league we are coming into because we've seen many sides think they can bounce back straight away and it's not happened that way.
"I'd love to sit here in a year's time and say we've won the league, but as long as we're in the Premier League, I couldn't care how we do it."
'My ambition is to get West Ham back to the PL - I'm not thinking beyond that'
Bowen's contract has four years left to run, but The Athletic have reported a release clause has been inserted into the deal, which will kick in next summer, if West Ham fail to seal an immediate return to the Premier League.
Conversely, he will reportedly receive a significant bonus if the Hammers do win promotion.
For now, he is looking no further than the season ahead.
"You never know what's going to happen in football, but my dream, my ambition, is to get this club back to the Premier League," adds Bowen.
"When you start looking years in advance, you're not focused on what you want to do this season. I've made my decision to stay because I'm focused on the now. I'm living in the present, not years to come.
"In my head, we're going to make this happen. If that doesn't happen, you reassess it in a year's time."

Barely 200 kilometres from Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, where students and youth of the country came together in thousands to demand educational reform in India, a notice was served on a university, declaring that most of its built structures were illegal and would soon be demolished.
The institute, Mohammad Ali Jauhar University (MAJU), located in Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, was established in 2006 by the Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust, founded by Azam Khan, one of the founding members of the Samajwadi Party. Khan, a former MP and 10-time MLA from Rampur, was one of the most powerful politicians in the region until the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in 2017.
MAJU is recognised by the University Grants Commission (UGC) and holds minority institution status. However, its staff and student body comprise people from varied backgrounds and religious communities, vice-chancellor (VC) Prof Zaheeruddin and students themselves told Alt News.
On July 15, the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued a notice to the university declaring that 38 of its 40 buildings were illegal and would be demolished within 20 days. The university was told to carry out the demolition itself, failing which, the RDA would carry out the demolition while charging the university expenses. However, the demolition order was stayed on July 28 by the chairman of RDA and the Moradabad divisional commissioner, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, till August 10.
Only a day after the notice, on July 16, a ‘counselling camp’ was set up outside the university’s main gate, the VC said. On the same day, the UP Public Works Department (PWD) declared an internal road belonging to the campus as a public road while installing signage, he alleged.
On July 27, Alt News visited the 475-acre campus on the first day of the semester. The buildings — designed, according to the VC, in the image of the White House and Turkish mosques — looked grand but lifeless as several structures stood half-built with construction abandoned mid-way. An air of uncertainty loomed over the campus and on the faces of the very few students who were present.
Some students, who were protesting the demolition, told Alt News that a student delegation had met the DM and sought written assurance that the buildings would not be demolished until the matter was decided by the Supreme Court. The DM gave only a verbal assurance and declined to put it in writing, they said.
‘All Buildings Constructed Before RDA’s Jurisdiction’
Zaheeruddin, who served as pro-VC and chairman of the department of law at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) before joining MAJU in April 2025, said that a prior show-cause notice had been issued on June 28 seeking a response from the university on the demolitions.
The university’s response was deemed unsatisfactory by the RDA, which called for a physical meeting on July 14, attended by registrar SN Salam and the institute’s legal counsel. The authority only heard their arguments for five minutes, and the next day, the demolition order arrived, said Zaheeruddin, adding: “This was completely unexpected for us. Our classes were running, admissions were fully underway. Compared to the past two years, more admissions were happening this year.”
The VC told Alt News the 38 buildings were constructed before 2016, when the university grounds fell under the gram panchayat, not the RDA. The RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to cover the land only through a notification in September 2024, he said, asserting that the authority is retrospectively taking action against buildings. “All buildings they have mentioned were constructed by 2016, when RDA had no presence in this area at all,” he said.
He further highlighted that multiple regulatory bodies — UGC, Bar Council of India, paramedical and nursing councils — have inspected and approved the university’s infrastructure over the years as part of their accreditation process.
Missing Paperwork & The 2019 Raid
The VC, however, did not want to show the approved maps to prove the buildings’ legality citing legal proceedings. “The matter is before both the divisional commissioner and the Allahabad high court. The university’s lawyers have advised against discussing legal specifics,” he said.
On the other hand, Salam, the registrar, offered a different explanation for the missing paperwork. He claimed that during a state-ordered raid in 2019, when police forces were deployed on campus, large quantities
of documents were seized. “They took so many documents, and we don’t know where they took them or find out which documents they took,” he said.
Salam recounted the 2019 raid, “As police and district officials raided the campus, the VC was confined to one floor, the registrar to another, the accounts staff locked elsewhere. There were media reports that around 8,000 books stolen from a 200-year-old madrassa had been recovered from the university. But when the matter reached court, only 26 books were produced.”
Both the VC and registrar claimed that during the raid, several books were destroyed, many of which were hand-written manuscripts. They also claimed that 42 large cupboards, purchased from Kolkata, with receipts and transport documents, were shown as stolen property. Alt News could not independently verify the claims made by the VC and the registrar on the 2019 raid.
The Sudden ‘Counselling Camp’
Exacerbating the adminstration’s and students’ worries after the notice was served, was the sudden counselling camp, allegedly set up the very next day to encourage students to enroll in other universities.
Among those at the camp were officials from Guru Jambheshwar University, Moradabad — a state university whose campus construction began in March 2024, currently operating from a temporary campus with just two rooms built, and teachers from Raza Degree College, Rampur. Their task, the VC said, was to inform prospective students that MAJU would soon be demolished and that they should apply for admission at Guru Jambheshwar University.
“I felt terrible, they were maligning us right in front of us, sitting outside our campus. I was shocked that government teachers were doing this and the district magistrate had set up the camp while we are still a functioning university,” Zaheeruddin lamented.
Arguing that the counselling camp amounted to contempt of court, he mentioned that the administration wrote to the Rampur DM citing a 2019 high court stay order that specifically ordered that students and staff of the university must not be harassed. The camp was removed after two days, on July 18 evening.
The Students’ Plight
When Alt News visited the campus, the students, now thrust into indefinite anxiety over their futures, were sitting in protest in front of the main gate, demanding that the RDA withdraws the demolition. “We are protesting since July 18 because RDA should withdraw this order. There are 3,000-4,000 students studying here, don’t snatch the pen from their hands,” said a 5th-year student from Panipat, Haryana.
Students echoed the administration’s account on the ‘pattern’ of state action which haunted their campus. Every year during admissions, they said, new action or rumours would surface, discouraging parents and prospective students. “Every year, fear is planted in children’s hearts that the university will be shut down,” said another student.
A student from Bareilly said his brother studied at MAJU between 2014 and 2017. After that, the perception in his area was that the university had already shut down. When he arrived for admission in 2015, he was urged not to enrol by several people in and around the area, with claims that the fees were too high and the university could collapse at any time.
The students further claimed that district officials attempted to curb their protest as the SDM arrived at the protest site on July 18 around 10 PM with policemen and asked the students to move their protest inside the campus, away from the main gate. District-level intelligence wing officials also called several parents, urging them to get their children to stop protesting, students alleged.
The students said they raised the issue with the district administration, which assured them that such pressure tactics would not be applied. Another protesting student mentioned that he had written twice to Saurav Das, the chief spokesperson of the Cockroach Janta Party, but had received no response at the time writing this report.
Alt News is withholding the names of the students who spoke to us in order to protect their identity.
RDA Officials Evade Queries
When we reached out to the RDA, we were re-routed through four different officials. We contacted RDA’s vice-chairman Ajay Kumar Dwivedi, also the district magistrate of Rampur, under whose name the July 15 notice was issued. His personal assistant, Ankush, directed us to the RDA secretary, Nitin Madan. The secretary, after answering some of our questions, directed us to the tehsildar, Ranveer Singh, who spoke briefly and redirected us to RDA assistant engineer Manoj Sisodia.
According to every official, only two of the 40 buildings had approved maps, obtained from the panchayat before RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to the area. The remaining 38, they said, had no approval from any authority — the Zila Panchayat, gram panchayat, or RDA. This formed the basis of the demolition notice, they said.
Upon being asked whether the matter could be resolved through compounding, a process where illegal construction is regularised by paying a fine and obtaining retrospective approval, Singh said it had been considered but rejected because the land use at the university site is not permissible under RDA’s current master plan. Sisodia, on the other hand, said that the university had never submitted a compounding proposal to RDA. However, the VC told Alt News that the institute believed that compounding was something RDA would initiate.
Further, we asked whether RDA had issued demolition notices to any other structures in the 62 villages that came under its jurisdiction since September 2024. Madan said “many have happened” without naming a single case. Ranveer Singh added “it keeps happening from time to time”, also offering no specifics. Sisodia eventually admitted that notices issued to other parties are “confidential and that the university’s case attracted attention only because it is a larger structure”.
“The university is in the wrong, but considering everything, the government, higher authorities, the courts, have taken their decision,” Sisodia said while acknowledging the dire condition of the students if the demolition is carried out.
The Azam Khan-Aunjaney Singh Connection
Parellel to all this runs another storied controversy between Azam Khan and Aunjaney Kumar Singh. During the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, complaints were filed by the then assistant development officer (panchayat), Anil Kumar Chauhan, and local BJP leader Akash Saxena against Khan for alleged hateful and provocative remarks against the then DM of Rampur, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, and other BJP leaders.
This led to Khan’s conviction in October 2022 with three years of imprisonment and his subsequent disqualification from the UP state assembly. His conviction was later overturned and he was acquitted by a higher court in Rampur.
Formerly an IAS officer of Sikkim cadre, Singh, hailing from Mau district in UP, notably has been serving as a government official in the state for 11 consecutive years now, and is presently on his sixth extension, which is set to end on August 14. Interestingly, in April last year, Singh accepted Khan’s plea against the imposition of Rs 20 crore fine in another case related to construction of MAJU.
According to Zaheeruddin, the demolition hearing, which was supposed to take place on August 3 at the court of divisional commissioner, has been postponed to August 10, bringing under scrutiny the apparent pendulum swing in the official relationship between Singh and Khan — from the district administration’s actions during Singh’s tenure as Rampur DM that culminated in Khan’s conviction, to subsequent administrative decisions that provided relief in matters concerning Khan’s university, and now the stay on the demolition proceedings.
The Unanswered Question
Beyond the missing approvals and the land use dispute, there is a deeper contradiction that neither the university nor the RDA addressed. During the April 2025 hearing concerning the Rs 20 crore labour cess fine, Khan had argued before the divisional commissioner that 10 of MAJU’s buildings were constructed by the UP PWD and UP Nirman Nigam using MP/MLA development funds.
Khan had then received relief after the divisional commissioner’s court nullified the cess fine imposed by the assistant labour commissioner (ALC) of Rampur. The same court, under the same authority of Singh, has now served a demolition notice to the institute. A pertinent question emerges: If state agencies built these structures with public funds, how did construction proceed without the approved maps?
Four government offices, multiple courts, contradictory bureaucratic positions and years of litigation have turned MAJU into a case study in administrative uncertainty. Whether the buildings ultimately stand or fall will be decided in court. Until then, it is not politicians or officials who bear the immediate cost of this prolonged impasse, but thousands of students who continue to attend classes while wondering if the campus they study in will still exist by the time they graduate.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

North Korea slams US-South Korea military drills and threatens strong response
North Korea has threatened unspecified stern steps against the United States and South Korea, slamming their upcoming military drills as a war rehearsal that it claimed would be more provocative than last year
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea on Friday threatened unspecified stern steps against the United States and South Korea ahead of their upcoming military drills, which Pyongyang called a war rehearsal that would be more provocative than last year.
The warning is typical of the harsh rhetoric that North Korea often deploys ahead of major U.S.-South Korean military exercises and suggests the country could conduct more missile tests in coming days. Experts say North Korea has often used its rivals' drills as a pretext to ramp up its testing activities to expand its weapons arsenals and promote public support for leader Kim Jong Un.
The U.S. and South Korean militaries are to start their major summertime Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises Monday and have described their scope as similar to past years. The allies have said the 11-day exercises are meant to strengthen their readiness against North Korean threats and reiterated that they are defensive in nature.
In a statement carried by state media Friday, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry called the U.S.-South Korean training “a rehearsal for an aggressive war” that is triggering a different level of instability in the region.
“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” the statement said. North Korea “will more clearly express its stance on the enemies to cope with any threats and challenges through the responsible and decisive exercise of the right to legitimate self-defense.”
North Korea also said the drills would be of a “more serious provocative nature and dangerousness than last year” and involve all the military assets and war-fighting modes of the U.S. and South Korea, a claim that those countries haven’t said.
A U.S. military statement issued Friday said U.S. and South Korean forces will practice joint operations in complex scenarios, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and maneuver, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of prepositioned military equipment.
North Korea's neighbors detected two ballistic missile launches off the North's east coast in the past week. North Korea hasn’t commented on the launches, but outside experts assess they were likely meant to protest the U.S.-South Korean drills or upgrade its weapons systems.
Kim has ignored the U.S. and South Korea’s offers to resume diplomacy and focused on taking steps to bolster his nuclear arsenal since his diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. Experts say Kim will likely eventually aim to use his advancing nuclear program to win greater U.S. concessions such as extensive sanctions relief.
North Korea has expanded cooperation with Russia in recent years by supplying troops and ammunition to support its war against Ukraine in return for economic and military assistance. North Korea has also recently pushed to deepen ties with China, its biggest trading partner.

Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan on Friday (August 14, 2026) formally launched the ‘My Police Station’ project that aims to transform police stations into accessible and citizen-friendly service centres.
Speaking at the State-level launch of the initiative at Peroorkada police station premises in Thiruvananthapuram, Mr. Satheesan said the project sought to make the police a “friend” and a source of support for people, while retaining the deterrent role of the force against crime.
The programme, he added, should create a sense among citizens that the police station belongs to them and that the police would stand by them in times of distress.
The Chief Minister said the initiative was particularly important at a time when the nature of crime was changing rapidly, with cybercrime, drug-related offences and technology-driven crimes posing new challenges. The police force would have to equip itself with modern technology and investigative capabilities to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminals, he said.
Need for courteous behaviour
Mr. Satheesan also stressed the need for courteous behaviour towards people visiting police stations. Citizens approach police stations for filing complaints, reporting crimes and obtaining verification and other services. Women, children and elderly persons were among those who frequently visit stations, and they should be received with dignity and compassion, he pointed out.
Delivering the presidential address, Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala said the project was designed to transform all 484 police stations in the State into more welcoming and citizen-oriented institutions.
He pointed out that police stations should no longer be viewed as places meant only for criminals or people facing legal trouble. Like village and panchayat offices, they should function as public service centres that the people could approach for assistance.
He also announced a series of organisational changes aimed at making the police force more responsive. Sub-Inspectors would be given greater operational responsibilities by being appointed as Station House Officers (SHOs), while Circle Inspectors would take up supervisory responsibilities over selected stations. Notably, as many as 63 police stations would have women serving as SHOs under the proposed changes, he said.
The Home Minister said senior police officers would also be required to visit police stations regularly and submit reports so that shortcomings could be identified and corrective measures introduced.
He emphasised that police personnel should respect legal safeguards and Supreme Court directives relating to arrests and custody. With CCTV cameras installed in police stations, including lock-ups, the department must ensure that custodial violence and deaths did not occur, he said.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, Thiruvananthapuram Mayor V.V. Rajesh, State Police Chief Ravada A. Chandrasekhar, Home Secretary Minhaj Alam, and Additional Director General of Police and ‘My Police Station’ nodal officer P. Vijayan, and the Police Adviser to Home Minister A. Hemachandran were among those who participated in the programme.
